seo.title: Karmic tail 12 7 4 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 7 4 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Chariot and The Emperor in a couple, how the tail adds up and its story in The Captain's Daughter.

title: Karmic tail 12-7-4 in compatibility: whose blessing the couple is waiting for
short: An odd combination: the couple enters through a card of waiting and sacrifice, and its main task is a card of power. The karmic tail 12-7-4 in compatibility explains it like this. First the two wait for someone older to give their union permission (The Hanged Man). Then an outside force picks them up and carries them along (The Chariot). Only after that does the couple take on the real work: setting up its own order at home, one that belongs to both (The Emperor).

sections.h2: A novel that begins with a tail
paragraphs: The Captain's Daughter opens with a scene that is easy to skim past. A map of the world had been ordered from Moscow for little Petrusha. It "hung on the wall without any use at all", and the boy decided to turn it into a kite. His father walked in "at the very moment when I was fixing a bast tail to the Cape of Good Hope". (Quotations from the novel are our own translation.)

A tail tied to the Cape of Good Hope. It is a coincidence, but a happy one: in 91% of couples with the tail 12-7-4 the centre is The Star, and Waite gives that card a second reading — "hope and bright prospects". The same opening scene already holds everything the tail is made of: a sheet of paper hanging idle, an attempt to fly, and a father who decides everything for everyone in one day. He pulled his son by the ear and threw out the French tutor that same day: "And that was the end of my education." When the son was going on seventeen, the father read the Court Calendar and sent him to serve not in St Petersburg but in the Orenburg steppe.

From there the novel is the story of one couple and one question. Blessings in it are asked for and refused, seen in a dream, given under fire, repeated by the wrong mouth. The order of the cards follows the order of the novel: a love waiting for the father's yes (The Hanged Man), a revolt and journeys by kibitka, a covered sledge (The Chariot), a trial and the Empress (The Emperor).

sections.h2: A clue in the numbers: a tail no single person can have
paragraphs: A couple's tail is added up point by point: one partner's entry with the other's entry, middle with middle, main task with main task; any sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Example: the dates 07.08.1976 and 05.11.1975.

For the first date the day is 7, the month 8, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. The karmic task is 7 + 8 + 5 = 20, the centre of the chart 7 + 8 + 5 + 20 = 40 → 4, the entry of the tail 20 + 4 = 24 → 6, the middle 20 + 6 = 26 → 8. The personal tail is 6-8-20.

For the second date the day is 5, the month 11, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The karmic task is 5 + 11 + 22 = 38 → 11, the centre 5 + 11 + 22 + 11 = 49 → 13, the entry 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, the middle 11 + 6 = 17. The personal tail is 6-17-11.

The first clue is in the middle. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is not added up but derived from the two ends: entry plus task. 12 and 4 would give 16, The Tower, so no birth date has 12-7-4 as a personal tail. In a couple, both partners bring the middle: it is the sum of their two personal middles. Where a single person would have The Tower between waiting and power, the two of them have The Chariot.

And they bring it in equal shares. In every couple with this tail the two personal middles add up to exactly 25. There are four such sums: Justice and The Star (8 + 17), The Fool and The Empress (22 + 3), Judgement and The Hierophant (20 + 5), The Chariot and The Moon (7 + 18). Each partner carries half of the road.

The second clue is in what is missing. The tail 12-7-4 comes from four pairings of personal tails: 6-17-11 + 6-8-20 (56% of such couples), 3-22-19 + 9-3-21 (31%), 6-20-14 + 6-5-17 (10%), 3-7-22 + 9-18-9 (3%). Neither The Hanged Man nor The Emperor appears in any of these personal tails, and The Chariot appears only in the last, rarest one. In 97% of such couples all three cards are born only in the sum: neither partner brings them ready-made.

The third clue is where The Emperor does live. A person whose personal tail is 6-8-20 always has 4 in the centre of the chart, their comfort zone. So in 56% of couples with the tail 12-7-4 the card of the main task already sits in the centre of one of the two, as it does for the date 07.08.1976. For one of them order is home ground; for the other it is a task. That makes neither of them the boss or the one to blame: the task is shared, they simply start talking about it in different languages.

The rest comes from the site's engine. The couple's centre, its atmosphere, is The Star in 91% of cases and Justice in 9%. No birth date has The Star in the centre of a personal matrix: only a couple can have this card there. The couple's values are The Lovers in 86.6% of cases and The Devil in 13.4%. The tail occurs in roughly one couple in 257 (0.388%), which puts it 64th of the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: Entry: "Without their blessing there will be no happiness for you"
paragraphs: The Belogorsk fortress turns out to be a hamlet behind a log fence. "But where is the fortress?" Grinyov asks the coachman. "Why, right here." Here, where nothing happens, love begins. Wounded in a duel, Grinyov proposes to Masha, and her first question is not about feelings: "won't your family stand in the way?"

The obstacle arrives by letter. The father gives "neither my blessing nor my consent" and promises "to teach you a proper lesson, like a little boy". Grinyov is ready to do without his father: they will throw themselves at the feet of Masha's parents, marry, and win his father round later. Masha refuses: "I will not marry you without your parents' blessing. Without their blessing there will be no happiness for you. Let us submit to the will of God. If you find the one meant for you, if you come to love another — God be with you, Pyotr Andreich."

The whole entry of the tail is in this scene. The two share one wish: that their union should be right, permitted. That is their common language: both are ready to wait, both are ready to step back for the other's sake. And the same wish turns into resistance. Masha almost stops speaking to him; Grinyov "sank into a gloomy brooding, fed by solitude and idleness". The love has not ended — it is hanging. Later, when Pugachev hands Masha over to him, she will say again that she will be his wife only with his parents' consent. And Grinyov "did not contradict her": by now it is his language too.

In Waite's divinatory list for The Hanged Man the words stand side by side: "Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice". Of Masha, Pushkin writes that she "was gifted in the highest degree with modesty and caution". Sacrifice rings out at every step of the novel: "at least you be happy", says Masha; under the gallows, Savelich, the old servant, begs to be hanged instead of his master.

Lisovskaya says of the twelfth energy in a couple what Pushkin showed through the plot: such couples take a long time to commit, and for marriage they need a push from outside. Grinyov describes it himself: he was pulled out of his brooding by "unexpected events" that gave his soul "a strong and salutary shock". That shock was the Pugachev rebellion. Benebell Wen gives The Hanged Man one more reading — "the unsettling calm before a storm". In the novel the storm is literal: a blizzard and a revolt.

Today this entry looks ordinary. The two have been together for three years, and the wedding keeps being put off: let Mum get used to it, let the renovation finish, let Dad stop calling it a whim. Grinyov fears the same thing — that his father will look on his love "as a young man's whim". Both are sure that waiting is noble. Each has given something up for the other: one turned down a move, the other a new job, and neither said it out loud. In the heavy version of the same card, one partner holds the relationship together with all their strength, hears only reproaches in return and cannot leave, while the parents decide about children and moving. The entry to the task is the first question the couple asks itself: whose yes are we waiting for, and what will change when it comes?

sections.h2: Middle: a guide who knows the road
paragraphs: The Chariot turns up in the novel before the love does, in the second chapter. Grinyov is travelling to his post, and a blizzard sweeps over the steppe. The coachman stops: there is no road. A stranger steps out of the snowstorm, and his first advice is to wait: "Better to stop here and wait it out; maybe the storm will die down and the sky will clear, and then we'll find the road by the stars." A minute later he climbs onto the coachman's seat himself: he has caught a smell of smoke, there are houses nearby — "turn right and drive on".

The whole move from the entry of the tail to its middle is in this one remark of the guide. First wait it out, then suddenly drive, and the one holding the reins is not the one travelling. And the stars he promises to steer by stand in the centre of 91% of these couples.

In thanks, Grinyov gives the vagabond his hareskin coat, and Savelich grumbles that "he'll drink it away at the first tavern, the dog". Later this vagabond takes the Belogorsk fortress under the name of Emperor Peter III, and Grinyov, with a noose already round his neck, is let go from under the gallows. Grinyov sums it up himself: "a child's sheepskin coat, given to a vagabond, was saving me from the noose". A gift given early on the road, with no thought of return, came back as rescue.

Then the guide carries him out once more. Orphaned Masha is held under lock and key by Shvabrin, who is forcing her to marry him. The general in Orenburg will not give soldiers and advises him "to have patience". Grinyov rides out to the rebels on his own, is caught, and decides that "providence" has brought him to Pugachev a second time. In the morning the two of them get into the kibitka; "the bell rang out, and the kibitka flew". Grinyov describes his position more precisely than any reading could: "I am an officer and a nobleman; only yesterday I was fighting against you, and today I am riding in the same kibitka with you, and the happiness of my whole life depends on you."

Waite's divinatory list for The Chariot opens with "Succour, providence" and goes on: "also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble". Reversed, the first word is "Riot", followed by "quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat". The novel runs through this list almost entirely: the rescue of an orphan, providence, war, the duel with Shvabrin, the commission of inquiry, the rout of the pretender. And the novel's most famous sentence is about the very first word of the reversed list: "God grant that we never see a Russian revolt, senseless and merciless!" The Russian word is bunt, a riot.

For the couple, something else matters more: here The Chariot is a relay. First Grinyov, finding himself before the self-proclaimed "sovereign", pleads with him for Masha. Then Masha travels to the real sovereign to plead for Grinyov. Each in turn carries the other out, and both times the road ends at the door of power, at the card of the main task. The numbers say the same: each partner brings half of the middle of the tail.

Among the tasks of The Chariot in a couple, Lisovskaya names the balance between career and relationship and the decision to move together. In Grinyov this is a single sentence: "Duty demanded that I go where my service could still be useful to my country... But love strongly advised me to stay with Marya Ivanovna." Later he chooses duty: he sends Masha to his parents and stays with his unit. The couple's move is settled, but one of them settled it: at night, after a talk with a friend, and in the morning Grinyov "told her of my intentions". She agreed.

The Chariot has a trap as well. In the same kibitka Pugachev tells a Kalmyk folk tale: the raven lives three hundred years because it eats carrion, the eagle only thirty-three because it drinks living blood, and the eagle decides: "rather than feed on carrion for three hundred years, better to drink living blood once, and then whatever God gives!" A couple with this tail recognises the temptation halfway along the road. In a rush job, a move, in rescuing each other, the two live more brightly than on an ordinary Tuesday, and the even life after the storm seems flat. Grinyov answers the pretender: "to live by murder and robbery is, to my mind, to peck at carrion." For a couple his answer means this: if the two feel alive only in trouble, that is not the eagle's flight, it is the same carrion.

Today the guide can be anything: a redundancy, an offer in another city, a flooded flat, a boss who will "sort it all out", a friend who knows where to rent. In a week the couple does what it has been putting off for years. One flies to a strange city to deal with the other's papers; a year later the other spends nights finding the first a lawyer and money.

sections.h2: The proxy father: when The Chariot takes The Emperor's seat
paragraphs: The most mysterious page of the novel is the dream Grinyov has in the kibitka during the blizzard. He dreams that he has come home and his father is dying. His mother leads him to the bed: "Andrei Petrovich, Petrusha has come... give him your blessing." "Instead of my father I see a peasant with a black beard lying in the bed, looking at me merrily." His mother urges him: "this is your posazhony otets; kiss his hand and let him bless you." Grinyov refuses, the peasant seizes an axe, the room fills with dead bodies, and the terrible peasant calls to him tenderly: "Don't be afraid, come under my blessing."

A posazhony otets, a proxy father, is the man who stands in for the real father at a wedding. The dream comes true in three steps. When Grinyov is taken down from the gallows and set before the pretender, the crowd shouts: "Kiss his hand, kiss his hand!" — he does not. In the Belogorsk fortress Pugachev, having freed Masha, offers it himself: "If you like, I'll be the proxy father." And when he lets them go, he blesses them with words the reader has already heard. Under fire, Captain Mironov blessed his daughter: "If a good man is found, God grant you love and concord." Pugachev, who hanged the captain, says the same: "Take your beauty; take her wherever you like, and God grant you love and concord!" The right words reached the couple from the wrong mouth.

Grinyov himself calls the dream prophetic, and that is one more line from Waite's list: the entry for The Hanged Man ends with "intuition, divination, prophecy". The entry of the tail sees what will happen in the middle.

Waite also explains the mechanism. His Chariot "is really the King in his triumph, typifying, however, the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence and not the vested royalty of the fourth card", The Emperor. Pugachev is The Chariot in pure form: power seized at full gallop. He knows himself how fragile it is: "My street is narrow; I have little freedom. My lads are too clever by half." The Chariot can carry a couple out of the blizzard, but it has no right to bless. The real emperor drew the same line, only on a title page. For his History of Pugachev, Pushkin travelled in 1833 to Berdskaya Sloboda, the rebels' capital, and questioned the old people there, and Nicholas I changed the title in his own hand to The History of the Pugachev Rebellion. The pretender was left a rebellion, not a history.

Hence the main lesson of the passage from The Chariot to The Emperor. The couple accepts the guide's help — the coat, the horse, the pass — but does not offer him a hand to kiss. Freed, Masha repeats what she said before: she will be a wife only with the consent of Grinyov's parents. This is not meekness. A proxy father cannot replace the real one, and she knows it.

Today the dream is easy to recognise. Someone carried the couple out of a crisis: a boss who gave work and a flat, a relative who paid off a debt, a friend they lived with for six months. Gratitude is natural. The danger comes when the rescuer starts to bless: to decide where the couple should live, when to marry and how to raise children. And the couple, out of The Hanged Man's old habit, waits for his yes.

sections.h2: The main task: two houses where one person decides
paragraphs: In a couple's tail The Emperor is the main task, and it is read mostly through what does not work. Pushkin shows it through two finished marriages, and between them the young couple has to build a third.

The first house is the Grinyovs'. The father, a retired major, receives the Court Calendar every year, a list of dignitaries and their ranks, and reads it with "a remarkable stirring of bile": "Lieutenant-general!.. He was a sergeant in my company!.." The mother knows this weakness and hides the book "as far away as possible", sometimes for months. Above this house stands someone else's hierarchy, and it holds together by one partner's quiet cunning and the other's temper: the father "liked neither to change his intentions nor to put off carrying them out". One reading of the calendar, and the son goes not to the Guards but to the steppe.

The second house is the Mironovs'. Here the wife rules: Vasilisa Yegorovna "looked on the affairs of the service as her own household business and ran the fortress exactly as she ran her little home". The commandant drills his soldiers "in a nightcap and a cotton dressing gown". He tries to hide a secret order from his wife and is caught out: "scheming is not for you". She has one answer to every objection: "are not husband and wife one spirit and one flesh?" The house is warm and funny, and in it, too, one person decides. When Pugachev approaches the fortress, the wife refuses to leave: "Together to live, together to die."

Pushkin sets the two marriages side by side: in one the husband rules, in the other the wife. Neither will do for the young couple, and the point is not who rules. The card is not about gender. It is about the fact that in both houses one person decides, and the other schemes, hides or submits.

Lisovskaya describes the minus of The Emperor in a couple with similar pictures: one decides for everyone, the rules are rigid, and feelings are hidden so deep that you cannot tell joy from anger. Her tasks for the couple sound like an answer to both houses: do not make rules that get in the way later, and learn to talk about feelings.

Among Waite's reversed meanings of The Emperor is the word "immaturity". The novel begins with it: "I lived as a nedorosl, chasing pigeons" — nedorosl, an idle overgrown minor. The main task of the tail is to grow from a nedorosl whose father picks his regiment into the master of his own house, without turning into the father with the calendar.

Today it looks like this. In one home "this is how it's done in our family" collides with "it was different in mine". A rule invented in a crisis — "one of us handles the money", "we don't mention bad news so as not to upset anyone" — lives on for years after the crisis is over. One partner hides from the other whatever irritates them, the way the mother hid the calendar. An argument about where to go on holiday becomes an argument about who is in charge here.

sections.h2: The trial: two silences and one plea
paragraphs: The most exact scene of the tail is the trial. Grinyov is arrested for his friendship with the pretender. He travels to Kazan resolved to tell the plain truth, and at the interrogation he falls silent: "It occurred to me that if I named her, the commission would summon her to answer." He "faltered and got confused", and the judges, who a moment ago had listened to him with goodwill, turn against him again. To protect Masha, he decided for her: her name will not be spoken. The price is a sentence of permanent exile to Siberia.

Masha, meanwhile, is living with his parents, and she too is silent: she "was deeply troubled, but kept silent". She guesses why he did not clear himself, blames herself and "hid her tears from everyone". Then one evening she announces that she is going to St Petersburg, and explains her plan only to Grinyov's mother, alone with her, and only "in part".

This is a pattern of the tail that is easy to mistake for love. The Hanged Man at the entry is sacrifice, The Emperor in the main task is decision. Together they make a decision for the other, taken in silence and with the best intentions. Grinyov decided for Masha that she had better not testify. Masha decided for Grinyov that she had to go. Each protects the other, and each rules alone.

That same evening Pushkin shows how power at home is changing. The father sits with the Court Calendar, "but his thoughts were far away, and the reading did not have its usual effect on him". For the first time the book of other men's ranks does not work. And the father who not long ago refused his blessing answers Masha: "Go, my dear! We do not wish to stand in the way of your happiness."

Next comes the garden at Tsarskoye Selo. On a bench Masha meets a lady "in a white morning dress, a nightcap and a dushegreika", a padded house jacket. The scene is generally thought to be drawn from Borovikovsky's portrait Catherine II Walking in Tsarskoye Selo Park (1794), where the Empress is dressed for home. And inside the novel the detail has an echo: in the seventh chapter, a robber looting Vasilisa Yegorovna's house dressed himself in her dushegreika. On the bench sits not a crowned sovereign but a woman in house clothes who is able to listen.

The conversation is short. "You are an orphan; no doubt you have come to complain of injustice and wrong?" "No, madam. I have come to ask for mercy, not for justice." When the lady coldly calls Grinyov "an immoral and harmful scoundrel", Masha, whom her mother called a coward, answers: "Oh, that's not true!.. It's not true, by God, it's not true!" And she tells everything: "if he did not clear himself before the court, it was only because he did not want to drag me into it." Grinyov's silence would have destroyed him. Masha's speech saved him.

The Empress answers in the language Waite places under The Emperor reversed: "Benevolence, compassion, credit". She is kind to the orphan, acquits the fiancé and says: "I am in debt to Captain Mironov's daughter." Power in this scene does not judge — it acknowledges a debt and shows mercy.

For the couple this gives a simple rule for the main task: in a dispute about power, ask for mercy, not for justice. Do not prove who is right under the law of the house; say what you are asking for. In 9% of couples with this tail the centre is Justice, and among its tasks Lisovskaya names the ability to admit one's own fault instead of accusing. For these couples Masha's sentence is doubly needed.

sections.h2: Under glass and in a frame
paragraphs: In the novel three papers hang on walls. The first is that map of the world in the Grinyovs' house, hanging "without any use at all" until the boy makes a kite of it. The second is in the Mironovs' house: "an officer's commission, under glass and in a frame". After the fortress falls, Grinyov sees it again, "like a sad epitaph to times gone by". The third is in the last paragraph. In the village where the descendants of Grinyov and Masha live, "they show a letter in Catherine II's own hand, under glass and in a frame. It is written to Pyotr Andreyevich's father and contains the acquittal of his son and praise for the mind and heart of Captain Mironov's daughter."

Put the three papers side by side and the whole path of The Emperor in this tail appears. First the wall holds a foreign world one wants to fly away from. Then a father's rank, earned but not the young couple's own. At the end, a paper about the couple itself. The letter is addressed to the father, the man who read the Court Calendar: instead of a list of other men's ranks he received a testimony to his daughter-in-law's mind and heart. The power that used to stand over the house now hangs on their wall. It no longer rules — it is shown to guests.

There is also a scene that is not in the printed novel. Pushkin wrote a chapter in which Grinyov, in the middle of the revolt, makes his way to his home village and finds his father, his mother and Masha tied up in the grain barn, locked in by the rebellious steward. Grinyov looks for a way out, and his father stops him: "Don't bother. I'm not the kind of master whose barns can be got into and out of through thieves' holes." The master built a barn so secure that he cannot get out of it himself. There could be no better picture of a rule that gets in the way later. The way out is found by the same father: when the barn is set on fire, he unlocks the door himself — "Now is the time!" — and leads everyone out through the flames. In the same chapter the parents finally bless the couple, and Grinyov advises the reader "while there is still time, to fall in love and receive your parents' blessing". Pushkin left this chapter out of the final text; it survives in the draft.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: "It's more frightening at home alone"
paragraphs: The atmosphere of this couple, its centre, is The Star in 91% of cases. Lisovskaya writes of The Star in a couple's centre that the partners often understand who they want to be only together, and open up, sometimes directly with each other's help. Masha is the best example. Her mother says of her in front of a guest: "Masha is a coward. To this day she can't bear the sound of a gunshot." On the rampart, as the rebels approach the fortress, her father asks her: "Well, Masha, are you frightened?" "No, Papa. It's more frightening at home alone." Later this coward travels to Tsarskoye Selo and argues with the Empress, not yet knowing who is in front of her. Grinyov travels the same road from the other side: from a nedorosl chasing pigeons to a man who withstands the gallows and the trial.

For the same Star, Lisovskaya also describes a shadow: the couple enjoys being in love but avoids responsibility and can fall apart as soon as marriage comes up; a partner is chosen under pressure from parents; home life is built on the parents' script. All of these are the novel's questions. The Star holds the couple while the entry and the middle run their course, but it does not settle the question of marriage or of someone else's script. That is The Emperor's work.

sections.h2: How a couple lives 12-7-4 in its plus
paragraphs: In its plus this tail resembles The Captain's Daughter at its best moments. The two know how to wait without losing each other. In the storm they do not abandon each other and take turns coming to the rescue. In the end they build a home of their own — grateful to their elders, but without their calendar. What helps:

ul: **Name whose yes the couple is waiting for.** Not "some day" but specifically: Mum's, Dad's, the boss's — or money for the wedding. And ask each other what will change when it comes, and what happens if it does not.

**Tell the guide apart from the father.** Whoever carried the couple out of the blizzard deserves a coat and gratitude, but not the right to decide how the couple lives from now on. Accept the help; do not offer a hand to kiss.

**Do not decide for the other in silence, even out of love.** Grinyov's silence at the trial nearly cost him Siberia; Masha's speech saved him. When the urge is to protect, first ask the other whether they want that kind of protection.
**Ask for mercy, not for justice.** In an argument about who is in charge, stop collecting evidence and say plainly what you are asking for.
**Write the house rules together and revisit them.** Especially the ones born in a crisis. A rule that cannot be got round "through thieves' holes" will one day lock in the person who made it.
**Do not live from storm to storm.** After rescuing each other, an ordinary Tuesday is not a flat life; it is what the journey was for.

**Change the elders by living, not by revolt.** Grinyov's father did not change his mind because of an argument: Masha lived in his house, and "it was impossible to know her and not love her". The narrator himself addresses the young reader: the best and most lasting changes are those that "come from the improvement of manners, without any violent upheavals".

paragraphs: The minus of The Emperor also means control, pressure and fear. If there are threats or violence in the couple, this is not a "task of the tail" to be endured: it calls for help — the local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man, entry to the task.** The couple's common language is waiting and giving way: "not now", "not without their consent", "for your sake I'll step back". This shared wish is how the couple enters the task, and the same wish becomes its first resistance.
**7 · The Chariot, middle of the task.** The road goes in jolts and most often starts with a push from outside. The two cover it in turns: each, at some point, carries the other out.
**4 · The Emperor, main task.** A law of their own at home: deciding together, not deciding for the other in silence, and not making rules that later lock both of them in.

intro: The whole path is written down in one Russian novel. Pushkin's Kapitanskaya dochka (The Captain's Daughter) is the story of who will bless Pyotr Grinyov and Masha Mironova. The father refuses. In a dream, a peasant with an axe offers to give the blessing. A pretender to the throne volunteers to stand in for the father at the wedding. The last word belongs to the Empress. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the numbers of the tail itself, in Waite, in Lisovskaya and in Pushkin. It is a tool for knowing each partner and the couple, not a forecast: the cards do not say what will happen, they show what the couple goes through and what it learns.

faq.q: Is the karmic tail 12-7-4 a bad sign for compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not rate compatibility and does not predict how a union will end: the method gives no percentages and no verdicts. It shows a task — the road from waiting for someone else's consent to an order of one's own at home. The difficulty of this tail lies in the minus of The Emperor: decisions made for both, rigid rules, a struggle over who is in charge.

faq.q: Why is there no personal karmic tail 12-7-4?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is derived from its ends: entry plus task. 12 and 4 would give 16, The Tower. In a couple the middle is the sum of two people's personal middles, and in every couple with this tail they add up to 25, that is, 7 — The Chariot.

faq.q: What does it mean if one partner has 4 in the centre of the chart?
faq.a: This happens in 56% of couples with this tail: a person with the personal tail 6-8-20 always has 4, The Emperor, in the centre. Order and rules are familiar ground for that partner and a new task for the other. That makes neither of them the boss or the one to blame: the task belongs to the couple.

faq.q: Where should a couple with the tail 12-7-4 start?
faq.a: With one conversation: whose approval are we still waiting for, and which rules in our home did we not make ourselves. Then agree which decisions are only ever taken together, and do not take them for the other, even to protect them.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among couple tails the cards 12, 7 and 4 occur only in the order 12-7-4: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, The Emperor as the main task.

report: Masha Mironova refuses to marry the man she loves for one reason: "Without their blessing there will be no happiness for you." The groom's father has withheld his blessing, and the union is left hanging. In Pushkin's The Captain's Daughter the story of the tail 12-7-4 is written down almost word for word. First the two wait for someone older to give their union permission (The Hanged Man). Then an outside force picks them up and carries them along (The Chariot). And the main task turns out to be power — an order of their own at home, shared by both (The Emperor).

report.h3: A common language that turns into resistance

report: The Hanged Man at the entry is what a couple with this tail wants together: for the union to be right, permitted. Both are ready to wait, both are ready to step back for the other's sake. Masha lets him go: if he finds the one meant for him, if he comes to love another, "God be with you". When she repeats her condition, Grinyov "did not contradict her". This is their common language, and it is also the first resistance. Masha almost stops speaking to him; Grinyov sinks into "a gloomy brooding, fed by solitude and idleness". The love has not ended — it is hanging.

Lisovskaya notes that such couples need a push from outside before they marry. Grinyov is pulled out of his stupor by "unexpected events" that gave his soul "a strong and salutary shock". Today it looks ordinary. The wedding is put off until Mum gets used to it and Dad stops calling it a whim. Each has quietly given something up for the other — a move, a new job — and neither has said so out loud.

report.h3: A guide who drives but cannot bless

report: The Chariot in the middle appears in a blizzard. A stranger advises them to "wait it out... and then we'll find the road by the stars", and a minute later climbs onto the coachman's seat himself. First wait, then suddenly drive, and the one holding the reins is not the one travelling. The guide turns out to be Pugachev. He lets Grinyov go from under the gallows for a hareskin coat given to him long before, and drives him in his own kibitka to free Masha. Grinyov puts it more precisely than any reading could: "only yesterday I was fighting against you, and today I am riding in the same kibitka with you, and the happiness of my whole life depends on you."

In this tail The Chariot is a relay. First Grinyov pleads with the self-proclaimed "sovereign" for Masha, then Masha travels to the real sovereign to plead for Grinyov. **Each in turn carries the other out**, and both times the road ends at the door of power.

But The Chariot has no right to bless. Grinyov dreams that a black-bearded peasant is lying in his dying father's bed, and his mother urges him: "this is your posazhony otets; kiss his hand" — the proxy father who stands in for the real one at a wedding. The dream comes true. Pugachev offers to be the proxy father himself and lets the couple go with the words "God grant you love and concord" — the same words with which Captain Mironov blessed his daughter under fire. The right words came from the wrong mouth. Grinyov does not kiss the pretender's hand, and Masha, already free, repeats that she will be a wife only with his parents' consent. Whoever carried the couple out of a crisis — a boss, a relative, a friend — deserves gratitude, **but not the right to decide how the couple lives from now on**.

report.h3: Deciding for the other in silence is power too

report: The main task is The Emperor, and it is read through what does not work. Pushkin shows two finished marriages. At the Grinyovs', the father reads the Court Calendar with "a remarkable stirring of bile" and decides for everyone, while the mother quietly hides the book away. At the Mironovs', the wife "ran the fortress exactly as she ran her little home". In one house the husband rules, in the other the wife, and gender is not the point: in both, one person decides, and the other schemes, hides or submits.

The most exact scene of the tail is the trial. Grinyov stays silent at the interrogation so as not to drag Masha into it, and is sentenced to permanent exile in Siberia. Masha, living with his parents, is silent too, and then decides on her own to go to St Petersburg. The Hanged Man at the entry is sacrifice, The Emperor in the main task is decision. Together they make **a decision for the other, taken in silence and with the best intentions**. Each protects the other, and each rules alone.

What saves them is not silence but speech. In the garden at Tsarskoye Selo, Masha tells an unknown lady in a nightcap: "I have come to ask for mercy, not for justice." When the lady calls the fiancé a scoundrel, the girl her mother thought a coward answers: "Oh, that's not true!" Power listens, shows mercy and admits: "I am in debt to Captain Mironov's daughter."

report.h3: What hangs on the couple's wall

report: In the Mironovs' house hung "an officer's commission, under glass and in a frame" — a father's rank, earned, but not the young couple's own. In the novel's last paragraph, the couple's descendants keep "under glass and in a frame" a letter from the Empress that contains "praise for the mind and heart of Captain Mironov's daughter". The power that used to stand over the house now hangs on their wall and no longer rules.

There is also the opposite picture, from a chapter Pushkin left out of the novel. The family is locked in its own barn, and the father tells his son: "I'm not the kind of master whose barns can be got into and out of through thieves' holes." A rule that cannot be got round locks in the person who made it.

ul: say out loud whose yes the couple is waiting for and what will change when it comes;
thank the guide, but not offer him a hand to kiss;
not decide for the other in silence, even out of love, but ask first;
in an argument about who is in charge, **ask for mercy, not for justice**;
write the house rules together and revisit them, especially those born in a crisis;
change the elders by living, not by revolt: Masha lived in the Grinyovs' house, and "it was impossible to know her and not love her".

report: If there are threats or violence in the couple, this is not a task of the tail to be endured: it calls for help — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

unit.meaning: Your task is your own order at home: decide together, wait for no one's blessing, never decide for each other in silence.
